\begin{proof}
Let $x\ne y$ be points of $X$, and put $\delta=d(x,y)>0$. Consider the distance-to-$x$ function
\[
f:X\longrightarrow\mathbb{R},\qquad f(z)=d(x,z).
\]
This function is continuous. Hence, because $X$ is connected, $f(X)$ is connected in $\mathbb{R}$. Since $f(x)=0$ and $f(y)=\delta$, the interval property for connected subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ gives
\[
[0,\delta]\subseteq f(X).
\]
The interval $[0,\delta]$ is uncountable, so $f(X)$ is uncountable. But the image of a countable set under any function is countable, and therefore $X$ cannot be countable. Thus $X$ is uncountable.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}
Since $X$ has more than one point, choose $x,y\in X$ with $x\ne y$, and let $\delta=d(x,y)>0$. Define $f:X\to\mathbb{R}$ by $f(z)=d(x,z)$. The map $f$ is continuous as the composition of the continuous metric map $d:X\times X\to\mathbb{R}$ with the continuous map $z\mapsto(x,z)$. Thus $f(X)$ is connected because $X$ is connected. Also, $0=f(x)$ and $\delta=f(y)$ belong to $f(X)$. Therefore, by connectedness in $\mathbb{R}$,
\[
[0,\delta]\subseteq f(X).
\]
Hence $f(X)$ is uncountable. If $X$ were countable, then its image $f(X)$ would be countable, a contradiction. Consequently, $X$ is uncountable.
\end{proof}
